title: CRLA/319/2002 of RAJPAL and ANR. Vs STATE

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Criminal Appeal No.319 of 2002
1. Rajpal
2. Sahinder Giri
 Ö Appellants
Versus
State of Uttarakhand Ö Respondent
Mr. Navneet Kaushik, Advocate for the appellants.
Mr. V.K. Gemini, Dy. Adv. General (Crl.) for the State/respondent.
With
Government Appeal No.34 of 2006
State of Uttarakhand Ö Appellant
Versus
1. Vijendra @ Naval
2. Kunwar Pal @ Kukkan
 Ö Respondents
Mr. V.K. Gemini, Dy. Adv. General (Crl.) for the State/appellant.
Mr. Mohd. Umar, Amicus Curiae for the respondents.
Honíble Servesh Kumar Gupta, J.
 This judgment will dispose of both the above-titled
appeals as the same have arisen out of a common judgment
and order dated 9.12.2002 rendered by learned Additional
Sessions Judge, Haridwar in Sessions Trial No.129 of 1998.
In the said trial, Rajpal (A1), Bijendra @ Naval (A2),
Sahendra Giri (A3) and Kunwar Pal @ Kukkan (A4) [all real
brothers] were tried for the offences u/s 308/34 and 506
IPC. The trial resulted into the conviction of A1 and A3 for
the offences of section 308/34 IPC, wherefor each of them
has been sentenced to five yearsí rigorous imprisonment. At
the same time, A2 and A4 were acquitted from all the
charges levelled against them.
2. Having heard the arguments for and against, it
transpires that on the relevant date and time, a quarrel
erupted between PW4 Ishtiyaq (injured) and A1 while the

2
latter was cutting boundary wall, separating his agricultural
field from that of PW4. PW4, feeling aggrieved by the said
action on the part of A1, resisted and asked him not to cut
the boundary wall making it narrow. A1 then exhorted his
brother A3, present nearby, to kill PW4. On such
exhortation, A3 as well as A1 gave blows of Lathi on the
head of PW4. It has further been deposed by the injured
that meanwhile A2 and A4 also arrived at the spot having
Lathis in their hands and they assaulted him too. The
incident was witnessed by all the persons who were working
in their agricultural fields including PW5 Yasin, PW6
Mursaleem and one other Sageer. Injured was then shifted
to Roorkee hospital by his brother Ashfaq (PW1) where he
was treated for quite sometime. The first information report
could be lodged next day on 12.7.1996 at 4:30 PM.
Chargesheet was submitted as a result of investigation
against A1 to A4 for the offences of section 308/504 IPC.
However, the Charge was levelled for the offences of section
308/34 and 506 IPC, which resulted into the findings of the
lower court, as afore-stated.
3. Learned counsel has pointed out that in fact PW1
is not the eyewitness of the incident. He is the informant
and real brother of PW4 (injured). In paragraph no.2 of
chief-examination, PW1 has deposed that his injured
brother Ishtiyaq was brought in the village by Sageer,
Mursaleem and Yaseen. PW1 then carried his brother to the
hospital from the village. He was apprised about the
incident by all these three witnesses and also by his brother.
So, this is enough to show that PW1 was not present at the
spot. Eyewitness Sageer has not been produced by the
prosecution during the course of trial whereas another
eyewitness Yaseen (PW5) has become hostile. The conviction
of the appellants has been based by the court below on the
testimony of PW4 and PW6.

3
4. The following injuries were found by the doctor on
the body of PW4 which are as under: -
A. ìAbrasion 2 cm x 1 cm on left side head, 11 cm
above left ear, surrounded by fr. swelling 8 cm x 6
cm, kept U.O. and ad. X-ray.
B. Contusion 21 cm x 3 cm on left side back upper and
middle part, Kept U.O. and X-ray.
C. Contusion 23 cm x 31⁄2 cm on right side back 13 cm
below inferior angle of scapula.
D. Contusion 8 cm x 3 cm on right side back 18 cm
below and lateral to injury no.3.
E. Contusion 13 cm x 31⁄2 cm on right side back upper
part.
F. Faint contusion 3 cm x 1 cm on back and upper part
of right upper arm.
Opinion- Injuries no.1 and 2 kept U.O., ad. X-ray, others
simple in nature, all caused by hard and blunt object and
are fresh in nature.î
5. On being x-rayed of injury nos.1 and 2, it was
found as under: -
ìA. Skull- Long linear fracture seen in left parieto-fronto- temporal bone.
B. Left side back upper and middle part Chest- No
fracture seen.î
6. Learned counsel has drawn the attention of the
Court towards some discrepancies, incongruities and
contradictions in the statement of PW4 with that of PW6.
The Court cannot be oblivious of the fact that the evidence
of PW4 was recorded after more than five years of incident
and PW6 could be examined after more than six years. So,
after lapse of such a long time, there is no evidence which

4
can be found without any contradiction or discrepancy. The
existence of such minor contradictions in the testimony of
witnesses more evidently makes their evidence believable.
Two rustic villagers cannot be supposed to be identical in
their remembrance on all minute details of incident which
occurred six years ago.
7. It has been argued that the Investigating Officer
in the site map has shown the fields of sugarcane around
whereas the field of A1 was having ëCharií (a grazing fodder
of cattles). This is again a contradiction in the site map from
that of the oral testimony of the witnesses. But it is not of
such degree which strikes the roots of veracity of incident.
8. It was next argued that injured could have been
taken to the first available hospital at Landhora or then at
Mangalore but ignoring both these hospitals, he was shifted
to Roorkee by PW1. This argument does not hold any water
for the reason that the injured was being carried in a Tractor
of their own. So, it was quite natural for PW1 to carry his
seriously injured brother in a hospital having better
facilities. The hospital in Roorkee certainly would have
better medical facilities than those two hospitals which came
on the way. Thus, there was nothing wrong on the part of
PW1 to carry his brother to the hospital at Roorkee rather
than to get him admitted in a hospital having lesser
facilities.
9. The Court has also considered the acquittal of A2
and A4 which is mainly based on the contradictions in the
statements of witnesses that these assailants sometimes
were attributed the role of having Lathis in their hands but
another witness has disclosed that they were armed only
with a Khaluwa (a thick baton). Their presence on the spot
is also doubtful for the reason that there is nothing on
record suggesting their presence along with the present

5
appellants. So, the Trial Judge recorded the finding of
acquittal in respect of A2 and A4, to which this Court also
concurs. There is no scope of interference with the said
finding arrived at by the trial court.
10. It has further been argued by learned counsel for
the appellants that no offence of Section 308 IPC is made
out. The premise behind such argument is that the
assailants did not have any common intention or knowledge
to commit the culpable homicide. Here, this Court is unable
to agree with the said contention because the definition of
culpable homicide, as envisaged u/s 299 IPC, does not
necessitate the existence of intention to cause the death
always. If the assailants had the knowledge that their act is
likely to cause death, then their action will be covered what
has been adumberated u/s 299 IPC. The blows of Lathis by
appellants Rajpal and Sahinder Giri, causing long linear
fracture in the left parieto-front-temporal bone of injured, is
enough to draw the assumption that they certainly would
have knowledge to the effect that their such action would
cause the death of injured. Although they did not have any
common intention but the common object was there, and
that object was made up in their minds at the spur of
moment.
11. At last, learned counsel has prayed clemency of
the Court that almost 18 years have elapsed from the
incident and all the parties are neighbours to each other.
So, if the appellants are made to suffer the rigorous
imprisonment, as long as for five years, then that may be a
cause of animosity between the parties. It was further
submitted that appellant Rajpal is almost on the death bed.
12. So, looking to the above-aspects, the Court
though maintains the conviction of both the appellants for
the offence u/s 308/34 IPC, but reduces their sentence to

6
that of one yearís rigorous imprisonment with fine of
Rs.5,000/- against each of them. In default of payment of
fine, the defaulter will undergo three monthsí additional
imprisonment. The period already undergone by the
appellants shall be adjusted from the sentence so modified
by this Court. Appellants are already in gaol in compliance
of the non-bailable warrants directed to be issued by this
Court. They shall serve out the modified sentence.
13. With the modification, as above, CRLA No.319 of
2002, preferred by the appellants Rajpal and Sahinder Giri,
is disposed of. At the same time, the appeal preferred by the
State, bearing GA No.34/2006, is dismissed in view of the
reasons stated in paragraph no.9 of the judgment.
14. Let a copy of this judgment and order along with
LCR be transmitted to the court concerned for compliance.
(Servesh Kumar Gupta, J.)
23.04.2014
Rdang
